text: Why does the book recommend forming a hypothesis before changing code?
choices: Because version control makes it expensive to revert speculative changes.
Because a change made without a prediction teaches you nothing when it works, and leaves you unable to distinguish a fix from a coincidence.
Because changing code without a hypothesis risks introducing a second bug.
Because hypotheses can be tested automatically, while changes must be verified by hand.
explanation: "I changed something and the error went away" is the state Chapter 35 identifies as the difference between people who get steadily better at this and people who plateau. A prediction turns each edit into an experiment with an outcome you can learn from — and when the prediction is wrong, that is more informative than when it is right, because your model of the program has just been corrected.
